content: The Stop TB Partnership was founded in the year 2000 with the primary objective of eradicating tuberculosis (TB) as a public health issue and ultimately achieving a world free of TB. It is a collaborative network that includes international organizations, governments, donors from both public and private sectors, non-governmental organizations, and individuals who are committed to this shared goal. The origins of the Stop TB Partnership trace back to the Stop TB Initiative, which was established after the First Ad Hoc Committee on the Tuberculosis Epidemic convened in London in March 1998. This initiative culminated in the Amsterdam Declaration to Stop TB in March 2000, a pivotal moment in global TB control efforts. The declaration called for urgent action from ministerial delegations representing 20 countries with the highest TB burden. Later that year, the World Health Assembly endorsed the creation of a Global Partnership to Stop TB and set two ambitious targets for 2005: diagnosing 70% of all individuals with infectious TB and curing 85% of those diagnosed. In October 2001, the First Stop TB Partners' Forum was held in Washington, D.C., where the Global Plan to Stop TB was launched, serving as the strategic framework for the partnership's collective actions. The Second Stop TB Partners' Forum, held in New Delhi in March 2004, resulted in the New Delhi Pledge, which reaffirmed commitments to the 2005 targets and laid the groundwork for a second global plan aimed at achieving the Millennium Development Goals for TB by 2015. The Stop TB Partnership has grown from its modest beginnings into a comprehensive global coalition. It unites organizations and individuals dedicated to both immediate and long-term strategies to control and eventually eliminate TB as a global health threat. The partnership has organized itself into specialized Working Groups to address seven critical areas: DOTS Expansion, TB/HIV co-infection, multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), development of new TB drugs, vaccines, and diagnostics, as well as advocacy, communication, and social mobilization. These collaborative mechanisms have allowed the partnership to expand its reach, implement work plans, and support countries in accelerating their TB control efforts, as outlined in the Amsterdam Declaration. The vision of the Stop TB Partnership is to create a world free of TB. The organization envisions that children born in the 21st century will witness the elimination of TB within their lifetimes. The partnership is a global movement aimed at catalyzing social and political action to halt the unnecessary spread of TB worldwide. By 2005, the goal was to diagnose 70% of individuals with infectious TB and cure 85% of them. By 2015, the aim was to reduce the global burden of TB (in terms of deaths and prevalence) by 50% compared to 1990 levels. By 2050, the ultimate goal is to reduce the global incidence of TB to less than one case per million population, effectively eliminating TB as a public health problem. The mission of the Stop TB Partnership is multifaceted. It aims to halt the transmission of TB, reduce the social and economic inequities caused by the disease, and develop and implement innovative preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic tools and strategies. To achieve these objectives, the partnership has outlined several goals: 1. Promote the broader and more effective use of existing strategies to interrupt TB transmission. This includes increasing access to accurate diagnostic methods and effective treatments by accelerating the implementation of DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course) to meet global TB control targets. It also involves improving the availability, affordability, and quality of anti-TB medications. 2. Develop strategies to address emerging challenges, such as adapting DOTS to prevent and manage multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and mitigating the impact of TB in individuals co-infected with HIV. 3. Accelerate the elimination of TB by fostering research and development of new TB drugs, diagnostics, and vaccines. Additionally, the partnership seeks to promote the adoption of these new tools by ensuring their appropriate use, accessibility, and affordability. The World Health Organization (WHO) plays a dual role within the Stop TB Partnership. As a leading agency, WHO provides guidance on global TB policy and maintains a permanent presence on the Stop TB Coordinating Board. Furthermore, WHO serves as the housing institution for the Stop TB Partnership Secretariat, which benefits from WHO's administrative, financial, and human resource management systems. The secretariat operates under WHO's rules and regulations, with necessary adaptations to meet the specific needs of the Stop TB Partnership.
